rounds.proof_sketch: Original: skip if blockCol < blockRow. Mutated: skip if blockCol*32 < blockRow-32. When mutant doesn't skip but original does (blockCol < blockRow AND blockCol*32 >= blockRow-32), the loop 'for(tile=blockRow; tile<=blockCol; tile++)' has blockRow>blockCol, so it never executes → sum=0. Write section: col<row in element coordinates → writes 0.0f. Since C is initialized to zeros, result is identical. The converse (mutant skips, original doesn't) is mathematically impossible for non-negative blockCol/blockRow.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes which blocks are skipped early versus which proceed to compute zeros. For any block where blockCol < blockRow (original skip condition), the inner loop 'for (int tile = blockRow; tile <= blockCol; tile++)' never executes because blockRow > blockCol makes the loop condition false immediately. This leaves sum = 0.0f. The write section then checks 'if (col >= row)' and writes 0.0f when col < row. Since C is initialized to torch::zeros, these blocks contribute nothing regardless of whether they're skipped early or processed. The mutation creates a semantic no-op: blocks that avoid the early return still produce identical output because subsequent code paths handle them equivalently.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is truly unkillable under value-level testing. The equivalence is structural/semantic, not value-dependent. The early-return guard is redundant because: (1) the loop bounds prevent computation for lower-triangular blocks, and (2) the output section explicitly zeros lower-triangular entries. No input values can create observable differences.
rounds.recommendations: When mutation testing kernel optimizations, verify that early-return guards are not redundant with subsequent bounds checks. This kernel has triple redundancy for lower-triangular handling: early block skip, loop bounds, and output masking. Consider removing redundant guards or consolidating logic to make mutations in these areas more detectable.
